title: Cancer Misinformation and Harmful Information on Facebook and Other Social Media: A Brief Report
screen_reason: CONTENT prevalence: two cancer content experts judged the veracity of the primary medical claims in each of the 200 most popular social-media cancer-treatment articles, and the paper reports the share classified as misinformation with its denominator (32.5%, 65 of 200).

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language articles; US-based author team)
estimates.platform: News articles and blogs posted on Facebook, Reddit, Twitter or Pinterest (96.7% of engagements were Facebook)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most popular social-media articles on the 4 most common cancers that expert reviewers classified as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 200 unique most-popular English-language articles (top 50 for each of breast, prostate, colorectal and lung cancer) identified with BuzzSumo and posted on Facebook, Reddit, Twitter or Pinterest between January 2018 and December 2019
estimates.definition: Two content experts rated each article's primary medical claims on a 5-point factuality Likert scale; the two raters' scores were summed and an article counted as misinformation if the summed score was >= 6, i.e. covering 'mixture both true and false', 'mostly false' and 'false' information
estimates.misinfo_def: “Misinformation was defined as summary scores greater than or equal to 6, representing “mixture both true and false,” “mostly false,” and “false” information”
estimates.source_quote: Of 200 total articles, 32.5% (n ¼ 65) contained misinformation and 30.5% (n ¼ 61) contained harmful information.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (quoted); same figure in Results paragraph 3 (p. 1037) and Table 1 (p. 1038)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two National Comprehensive Cancer Network panel members served as content experts for each cancer site (8 expert physicians in total); each article's primary medical claims were rated on two 5-point Likert scales adapted from published factuality and social-media credibility instruments; Cohen kappa for misinformation = 0.63 (95% CI 0.50-0.77), for harmful information = 0.66 (95% CI 0.52-0.80).
estimates.moderator_quote: Using web-scraping software (Buzzsumo.com) (12), we searched for the most popular English language articles containing relevant keywords for the 4 most common cancers (breast, prostate, colorectal, and lung). These articles include any news article or blog posted on Facebook, Reddit, Twitter, or Pinterest between January 2018 and December 2019. ... The top 50 articles from each cancer type were collected, representing 200 unique articles.
estimates.notes: The text file renders '=' as '¼' and the kappa symbol as 'Œ' (OCR artefacts); quotes are copied as they appear in the text. Topic coded health_other (cancer treatment), denom_scope topical with denom_selection=curated because the sample is the rank-truncated top 50 articles per cancer type. Country not stated anywhere in the text - only 'English language' - so coded Global. year set to 2019, the end of the January 2018 - December 2019 article-posting window (expert review itself is undated). The Results sentence carrying the same value and the kappa is “Following expert review, 32.5% (n ¼ 65; Œ ¼ 0.63, 95% confidence interval [CI] ¼ 0.50 to 0.77) contained misinformation”; the abstract sentence is quoted in source_quote because it is a single contiguous span.

missed_or_uncertain: Numbers seen but NOT extracted. (a) Harmful information: 30.5% (61 of 200) of articles contained harmful information (Table 1, kappa 0.66). This is a harm judgement, not a veracity judgement - a wholly accurate article can be coded harmful (e.g. economic harm) - so it is not a misinformation prevalence estimate and I created no row. An adjudicator may wish to record it as construct OTHER. (b) 'Among articles containing misinformation, 76.9% (50 of 65) contained harmful information' - again harm, and computed inside a misinformation-only sample; not a falsity share, so R3 (within_misinfo_content) does not rescue it. (c) The reason-for-rating breakdowns - misleading 28.8% (111 of 386), evidence mischaracterized 27.7% (107 of 386), unproven therapies 26.7% (103 of 386), and the harm sub-reasons out of 358 - have a denominator of SELECTIONS (multiple selections allowed per article), not articles, so they are not shares of content and cannot be pooled. (d) Article-source composition (traditional news 37.5%, nontraditional news 41.5%, personal blog 1.0%, crowd-funding 3.0%, medical journals 17.0%) describes the sample, not falsity. (e) No per-cancer or per-platform misinformation rate is reported, so I did not split the 32.5% - 50 articles were sampled per cancer but only the pooled falsity share is given, and INSTRUCTIONS forbid inventing sub-rows from a pooled number. JUDGEMENT CALL: breadth coded 'misleading' (the broadest option) because the numerator admits 'mixture both true and false' items, not only outright false ones.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. BuzzSumo web-scrape of the most popular English-language articles containing keywords for the 4 most common cancers, posted on Facebook, Reddit, Twitter or Pinterest between January 2018 and December 2019; top 50 per cancer type = 200 unique articles. Each article independently rated by 2 NCCN panel content experts for that cancer site on two 5-point Likert scales (factuality, harm); scores summed across raters. Cohen kappa 0.63 (95% CI 0.50-0.77) for misinformation and 0.66 (0.52-0.80) for harm. Engagement compared by 2-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum. Author-stated limitations: only the most popular English-language articles; possible incompleteness of BuzzSumo data; possible reviewer bias toward conventional cancer treatments.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation was defined as summary scores greater than or equal to 6, representing “mixture both true and false,” “mostly false,” and “false” information, and harmful information was defined as any rating by at least 1 reviewer of “probably harmful” and “certainly harmful” information.
rob.item10_quote: Of 200 total articles, 32.5% (n ¼ 65) contained misinformation and 30.5% (n ¼ 61) contained harmful information.
